claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits limited amorphous retention and limited glass formation.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complicated, multi-step thermal or crystallization response.
Approximately 5 at% B should be added while removing an equivalent total fraction of the transition metals.
Adding approximately 5 at% B will enhance the glass-forming ability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Adding approximately 5 at% B will improve the alloy's thermal stability during reheating.
B addition will enhance atomic packing.
The atomic-size mismatch introduced by B will increase topological frustration.
B addition will increase the alloy's chemical complexity.
B atoms are smaller than the relevant constituent atoms and are metalloid in nature.
B-induced packing frustration will increase the nucleation energy barrier.
The increased nucleation barrier will destabilize potential crystalline nuclei during fast cooling and suppress crystallization.
B addition will raise the onset temperature for crystallization during reheating.
After rapid quenching, the B-modified alloy will have a higher amorphous volume fraction than the baseline alloy.
During reheating, the B-modified alloy will exhibit a cleaner, more thermally stable exothermic crystallization peak than the baseline alloy.
The expected improvement should occur under rapid solidification, including rapid melt spinning and the stated arc-solidification processing.
The beneficial effect may be reduced at significantly slower cooling rates because competing crystallization is not bypassed.
If reheating is too rapid, B addition may not produce the predicted benefit.

The hypothesis is falsified if, under matched processing conditions, the B-containing alloy shows no statistically significant increase in amorphous fraction and/or no single higher-temperature crystallization exotherm relative to the baseline.
